title: Winding on
question: How does the camera know it has moved the film exactly one picture?
hook: After every picture you turn the green knob and exactly one picture's worth of film slides along. Too little and two pictures land on top of each other; too much and you waste film. No motor, no chip. The film does its own counting, with a row of holes older than cinema.

sections.title: Your guess first
sections.body: Take a picture, wind, take the next. Each picture is 36 mm long. If the camera winds 30 mm, two pictures overlap into a ghostly double. If it winds 60 mm, you lose a third of your roll to blank film. The camera has to get it right 36 times in a row, with nothing but plastic.
sections.q: How does the camera know it has moved exactly one picture?
choices: One turn of the knob is one picture
It guesses, and the lab sorts it out
sections.reveal: It measures the film. Counting turns can't work, and the next experiment shows why: film winds onto a roll, the roll gets fatter, and a fatter roll swallows more film per turn. By the model, one turn of the red spool takes in about 37 mm when it is nearly empty and about 63 mm when it is full. Same knob, same turn, wildly different lengths.

sections.title: The film carries its own ruler
sections.body:
Counting turns of a knob doesn't work: as film piles onto a spool, each turn takes in more. So the camera counts something that never changes.

Look along the edge of any 35 mm film: a row of little holes, 4.75 mm apart. One picture is 36 mm long plus a 2 mm gap: 38 mm. And 8 × 4.75 = 38.00 mm exactly. Eight holes, one picture, at the start of the roll and at the end.

The blue frame wheel has 8 teeth that sit in those holes. The wheel doesn't pull the film; the moving film turns the wheel. Eight holes go by, the wheel turns once, its white arrow comes home, and you stop.

One twist: this camera loads backwards on purpose. You wind the whole film out onto the red spool first, then each picture is wound back into the shell. Every picture you've taken is safe in the dark.

timeline.what: William Dickson, in Edison's lab, settles on film 35 mm wide with holes down both edges, for moving pictures.
Oskar Barnack runs movie film sideways for still pictures, 36 × 24 mm: the size of yours.
His camera, the Leica, goes on sale, and 36 × 24 mm spreads.
Film arrives in a small daylight-loading shell: the 135 cassette your camera takes.

sections.label: Why this piece exists

sections.title: Wind on, one picture at a time

sims.intro: The film from behind, drawn to scale. Take a picture, wind with the green knob, and stop when the blue arrow comes home.
sims.after: Every picture that arrived with the arrow home is exactly 38 mm from the last. The red knob's turns per picture kept changing; the frame wheel's never did.

sims.intro: The red spool's roll, end on: 5.9 mm radius empty, 10.1 mm full. Slide from full to empty and watch what one turn is worth.
sims.after: One turn moves 2 × 3.14 × the radius, and the radius grows with every turn: from 37 mm a turn to 63 mm. Count turns and pictures wander. Count holes and they don't.

sections.title: Wind until the arrow comes home
sections.alt: The blue frame wheel's dial with its white arrow, next to the big red knob
sections.caption: The blue dial goes round once for each picture.
sections.body:
After each picture, turn the small green knob until the arrow on the blue dial has gone once round. That's it: 8 holes, 38 mm, one picture. Keep your other hand off the big red knob, and never force either one: a stiff knob means a hand is on the other, or the film has reached its end.

Loading: about 25 turns of the red knob for a 24-picture film, 33 for 36.

sections.title: Nothing to wind, and a 35 mm ghost
sections.body: A phone has nothing to wind: its sensor is wiped and reused, many times a second for video, and its picture counter is just a number in memory. But the 36 × 24 mm picture lives on. Phone makers still describe their lenses as what they would be on 35 mm film: that's what '24 mm equivalent' on a spec sheet means.

sections.title: Why turns can't count pictures
sections.summary: one sum, with the real numbers
lines: 63.4 ÷ 37.1 = 1.71: the last turn takes 1.7 times the first
sections.body: A roll of sticky tape shows the same thing: its outer turns are much longer than its inner ones.

sections.title: A roll that grows
needs: a paper strip at least 1 m long, 2 to 3 cm wide
a thicker marker or glue stick
steps: Wind the strip tightly onto the pencil, one turn. Where it meets itself, draw a line across.
Keep winding, marking every turn, until the whole strip is on.
Unroll it and measure the gap between each mark and the next.
Plot the gaps on squared paper: turn number across, gap up.
Do it again on the marker and plot that line too.
sections.notice: The gaps grow steadily, faster on the fat marker. If each mark were a picture, the pictures would drift apart. That's why the camera counts holes.

items.q: Why can't the camera count turns of a knob to move one picture?
choices: The roll grows, so each turn moves a different length
Turns are too hard to count
items.why: A fatter roll takes in more film per turn. On the red spool, by the model, about 37 mm per turn empty and 63 mm full.

items.q: How many of the film's holes make one picture?
items.why: 8 × 4.75 mm = 38 mm: a 36 mm picture plus its 2 mm gap.

items.q: What turns the blue frame wheel?
choices: The film, moving past its teeth
items.why: The film pushes on the 8 teeth sitting in its holes. Eight holes pass, the wheel turns once, the arrow comes home.

items.q: Why wind the whole film out first and each picture back into the shell?
choices: Pictures already taken are safe in the dark shell
The film is stiffer that way
items.why: If the back opens by accident, only the pictures not yet taken are fogged.

items.q: About how many turns of the green knob wind a roll of 24 pictures back into its shell?
items.why: About 25 turns for 24 pictures, 33 for 36. Not one turn per picture: the roll changes size as it goes, which is the whole point of this lesson.

sections.title: Try it on your roll
sections.lead: Three frames in a row, to see the film move one picture at a time.
shots: A friend walks slowly toward you from about 6 m. Press.
Wind until the arrow comes home. Press again.
sections.look: On the negatives the three frames sit side by side with a thin, even gap between them. Frames that overlap mean a wind that stopped short.

sections.body: Knobs, a dial and a back that comes off. Every one is a gap. So why is the film not ruined?

links.title: 135 film
links.why: The film in your camera: sizes, holes and history.

objectives: Explain why counting turns of a knob cannot move film one picture at a time.
Show that eight holes 4.75 mm apart are 38 mm: one 36 mm picture and a 2 mm gap.
Describe how the film turns the frame wheel, and why the wheel turns exactly once a picture.
Explain why the film is wound out first and each picture wound back into the shell.
Work out one turn of a roll from its radius, and compare an empty spool with a full one.
materials: Per group of three: a paper strip at least 1 m long (till roll), a pencil, a marker, a ruler, squared paper, a calculator
A length of old 35 mm film or a spent film shell with its tail (any lab can give these), a magnifier
The class camera if built; otherwise the page on a projector
teach.exit_ticket: In one sentence: how does the camera know it has moved one picture? And one number: how many millimetres are eight holes? (38.)
teach.misconception: That a camera moves film one picture by turning a knob a fixed amount. In its place: a roll grows, so turns are not lengths; the film carries its own ruler, the holes; eight holes are one picture; and the film itself turns the wheel that tells you when to stop.

differentiation.support: Give a table with the radius already filled in (5.9, 8, 10.1) and only the multiplication to do. Use the roll sim's readouts as a check. For the Try card, pre-mark the first turn.
differentiation.stretch: The roll grows by about twice the film's thickness each turn. Use 5.9 mm empty and 10.1 mm full for 1368 mm of film to estimate the film's thickness (area of the ring = thickness × length: about 0.15 mm). Compare with a real film measured by a micrometer.
differentiation.access: The wind sim works from the keyboard (arrow keys turn the knob, Space takes a picture) and reports every picture in words. The Try card can be done in pairs with one person winding and one marking.

teach.safety: Open a loaded camera's back only after the arrow has stopped and three more turns are done, and only in the shade. Nobody forces a knob.

period.what: Show 'Your guess first'. Every student writes A, B or C. Class vote; most choose A. Do not correct yet.
Project the roll sim. Slide from full to empty; students call out the length of one turn each time.
Groups do the Try card (a roll that grows). Each group also looks at real film holes under a magnifier.
The film's ruler: the holes figure and the wind sim. Work the sum on the board line by line.
Pairs: the sum's check, then the quiz. If there is a loaded class camera, wind on one picture and watch the arrow come home.
Exit ticket, then back to the vote: who changed their mind?

questions.q: If the roll gets fatter, does one turn move more film or less?
questions.a: More: the distance round is bigger.

questions.q: The last turn moves 63 mm. How many holes is that? Would one turn be one picture?
questions.a: 63 ÷ 4.75 = about 13 holes: nearly two pictures. No.

questions.q: What is the distance from one hole to the next, and how did you measure it best?
questions.a: 4.75 mm. Measure ten holes and divide by ten: the error shrinks tenfold.

questions.q: Why could we open the back after the arrow stopped and three more turns?
questions.a: The film is all in its shell. Opened earlier, the pictures not yet wound in would be fogged.

questions.q: A roll has radius 8 mm. One turn?
questions.a: 2 × 3.14 × 8 = 50.2 mm, a bit more than one picture.
